chapter: Touring abroad and the future of music
title: Early jazz education and the GI Bill music schools
summary: Jazz study was once looked down on; early pioneers worked alone, and major music schools grew out of the GI Bill.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: School days: grades, teachers and leaving school

blocks.x: That's true. That's what you get in anything. But at least there is this going on now.
And heretofore, you could hardly find such a thing.
There never was, it wasn't allowed. It was looked down upon as the lowliest form.
Yeah. I remember, there was this one (inaudible) in San Francisco, at the College of at San Mateo, there was a guy there working his butt off in 1946.
Yeah, well, he's probably the earliest then.
Yeah, I mean, 'What's going on there,' but yet, he kept doing it. He didn't have any Com-patriots or anything, just forged ahead, helped a lot of people.

You know, if a lot of them just realized that some of the most important music schools in this country were built on a GI Bill, such as Berkeley and a lot of other places, they would never have been able to get into existence. It was a place to practice for guys who got out of the service. Nothing more or less.
